Annotations 71 LITTLE BUNNY 5 “She never raised her voice. She didn’t have to. The score was already on the board.” — Little Bunny LITTLE BUNNY 7 — I — The Room Where She Already Knew Before you walked through her door, she had already scored you. Not maliciously. Not with contempt. She had simply been doing this long enough to read the architecture of an

entrance—the way you set your bag down, whether you found a seat or waited to be pointed to one, the half-second pause before you said good morning. These were data. She was always collecting. Miss Patricia taught eleventh-grade English at a school where the hallways smelled like floor wax and old ambition. She had been there for nineteen years. She had outlasted four principals, two curriculum overhauls, one asbestos scare, and the brief administrative experiment of removing all classroom doors in the name of transparency. The doors came back. She had not moved. The PLT Framework—though she had never called it that—was already operating in her room. Every conversation had a structure. Every exchange had a purpose. Every student was being scored against a rubric no one had handed out, because the rubric was the relationship itself. You either understood that or you didn’t, and the ones who didn’t understand it usually realized it too late. This book reconstructs those conversations. Not to expose her, and not to mythologize her. She was neither villain nor saint. She was a practitioner. She operated with precision inside a room where most adults had given up on precision. That alone made her worth documenting. What follows is a scored record. ★ The first time I sat in her class I was sixteen and

certain I understood how rooms worked. I had already developed what I would later recognize as an early, untrained version of the Framework: I scanned for alignment, I read exits, I registered who held actual authority versus who held official authority. In most classrooms, these were different people. In hers, they were the same person, and that disoriented me. LITTLE BUNNY 15 — II — First Exchange The exchange happened on a Tuesday. Third week of school. She had asked the class to name a moment when language had changed the outcome of something real. Not a hypothetical. Something that actually happened. MISS PATRICIA 9 "Who wants to start? And before you answer — I want the real story, not the one that sounds good in class." PLT NOTE: High-positioning opener. Creates a double bind: if you perform, she’ll name it. Forces authentic disclosure. STUDENT (MARCUS) 6 "I told my mom I failed the chemistry test before she could find out from school. She took it better coming from me." PLT NOTE: Score 6: Honest, but structurally safe — ‘taking it better’ is outcome-focused, not language-focused. She’ll push. MISS PATRICIA 8 "That’s control, not language. You managed her reaction. What did you actually say to her — the sentence itself." PLT NOTE: Score 8: Precision redirect. She’s distinguishing strategy from

content. This is the PLT distinction in real time. STUDENT (MARCUS) 8 "I said, ‘Mom, I need to tell you something and I need you to let me finish before you say anything.’" PLT NOTE: Score 8: This is framing. Pre-emptive structural language. She will reward this. Watch. MISS PATRICIA 9 "Right. That sentence did work before the information arrived. Most people don’t know language can do that." PLT NOTE: Score 9: Doctrine delivery. She names the mechanism. This is teaching in three words: ‘before the information arrived.’ LITTLE BUNNY 23 — III — The Score You Didn’t See Coming She never posted scores publicly. That was by design. The score was something you felt before you understood it — a shift in her attention, a follow-up question that meant she had already processed your answer and found it insufficient, or silence that indicated she was letting you sit with what you’d just said. The PLT Framework defines scoring not as judgment but as calibration. A score is a reading of alignment between intent, language, and outcome. Miss Patricia scored constantly, without drama. She was not grading you as a person. She was reading the gap between what you meant and what you produced. The students who thrived in her room were the ones who learned to close that gap.

They became, over time, precise. They said what they meant. They meant what they said. They understood that vagueness was not a shield — it was a cost. LITTLE BUNNY 71 — VIII — Annotations What follows are the PLT annotations for the exchanges documented in this volume. Each score reflects the Framework’s three primary axes: Positioning (did the speaker establish or cede ground?), Language Precision (did the words match the intention?), and Timing (was the intervention placed at the moment of maximum leverage?). The composite score appears as a single integer from 1 to 10. Chapter II, Exchange 1 Opener: Score 9 She uses a double bind as her entry. The clause ‘not the one that sounds good’ pre-scores performative answers before they arrive. This is positioning through pre-emption. Extremely high-level. Chapter II, Exchange 3 Redirect: Score 8 Distinguishing strategy from content is a Framework-level move. She is teaching the students to see the layer beneath behavior. Most educators never access this layer at all. Chapter II, Exchange 5 Doctrine Delivery: Score 9 Three words — ‘before the information arrived’ — contain an entire curriculum unit. This is compression. The mark of a master practitioner is that they compress doctrine into ordinary speech without announcement.
